content_metadata.description: Analysis of domain percolation in a spinor Bose-Einstein Condensate.

qAndA.answer: A spin-1 system with three accessible spin levels.
qAndA.question: What type of spin system is being studied in this research?

qAndA.answer: The quenching process involves suddenly changing the quadratic Zeeman energy to a value where the condensate becomes unstable. It is implemented by rapidly changing the magnetic field applied to the system.
qAndA.question: What is the quenching process mentioned in the video, and how is it implemented?

qAndA.answer: It represents a percolating domain, which is a continuous region of positive spin domains that connects two opposite boundaries of the system.
qAndA.question: What does the blue highlighted area in the binary image at 1:35 represent?

qAndA.answer: They used a coherent spin rotation technique, which is a standard method in atomic physics experiments, to control the proportion of atoms in the positive spin state.
qAndA.question: How did the researchers vary the positive domain population in their analysis?

qAndA.answer: Heating of the system due to the quenching process is a significant challenge. They suggest using a carefully prepared initial state to minimize this heating.
qAndA.question: What is a key challenge the researchers identified for observing this behavior in experiments?

In this work, we theoretically explored the geometrical statistical properties of the
spindermains that form an equate spinner Bose-Einstein condensate.
A spinner Bose-Einstein condensate is an ultra-code guess of bosonic ashams in which each ash
has access to several different spin states.
In our case, we study a spin-1 system with three accessible spin levels.
The ashams in the condensate we consider also have theorem-ethetic interactions, which
means that these interactions favor the system magnetizing.
We consider the system prepared in an initial state that is un magnetized.
The quenches implemented by suddenly changing the quadratic Z-men energy to a value at which
this condensate is unstable, so that it forms easy access magnetic domains.
That is, spin domains that are aligned with or against the direction set by the Z-men
field.
In this simulation, we show the dynamics of a small, quasi-two-dimensional condensate undergoing
this evolution.
Starting from the un magnetized state, you will notice a small domains form.
Then, as time progresses, these domains tend to grow larger.
We analyze the structure of these domains once they form.
To do this, we have applied the ideas of percolation theory.
Notably, we focus our attention on the positive or upward pointing spin domains.
We can make a binary image by setting all positive domains to be white.
We examine if any of these domains percolate across the system.
Here is an example of percolating domain that connects from the lower boundary to the
top boundary.
This domain also happens to connect the left and right boundaries.
In order to explore percolation characteristics, we need to change the relative portion of
atoms in the positive domain and see how this affects the probability of a percolating
domain occurring.
In this work, we varied the positive domain populations using a coherent spin rotation,
a standard technique of atomic physics experimental to a box.
We find that the probability of finding a percolating domain varies smoothly as a portion
of positive atoms is varied.
Thus, identifying a smooth percolation transition.
Conducting a finite size analysis, we examine how this probability changes as the system
size increases.
This allows us to extrapolate to the thermodynamic limit, where the transition is discontinuous,
and hence identify the percolation threshold and the correlation length critical exponent.
In addition to showing that spin domain formation can be described by percolation theory, we
also examine the feasibility of studying this behavior in experiments.
That is, we examine factors such as the time dependence of domain growth and the continuous
nature of the spin density on the percolation analysis.
We also suggest a way to minimise heating from the quench by its preparing a sociable
initial stage.
We hope that this work will inspire experiments to make the first studies of percolation
in an ultra-called atomic gas.
